lines.text: A grating sends one colour into bright spots at particular angles. Their positions let you predict the wavelength and the possible diffraction orders.

For normally incident light, adjacent grating slits have spacing d. At angle theta from the straight through, zero order direction, their path difference is d sine theta. A bright maximum occurs when this equals a whole number n of wavelengths, d sine theta equals n lambda. Here n equals zero, one, two, and so on labels diffraction order on either side. Convert line density N in lines per metre to spacing with d equals one over N. Since sine theta is less than or equal to one, only orders with n lambda is less than or equal to d occur, count both sides and the central maximum when finding the total number of spots.
This extends double slit interference, path differences select constructive interference, while the many lines of a grating make the maxima sharp.

d sine theta equals n lambda for normally incident light. d is spacing between adjacent lines, theta is measured from the central direction. Orders are integers and satisfy n lambda is less than or equal to d. Two sided spot count is two n sub the maximum of, plus one when all orders are visible. Direct monochromatic light normally through a grating of known line density. Identify the central zero order maximum and a maximum of known order n. Measure its angle theta from the central direction, preferably on both sides. With a screen, measure grating to screen distance L and transverse displacement y, calculate theta equals inverse tangent of open bracket y over L close bracket. If density is given in lines per millimetre, multiply by one thousand for lines per metre and invert to find spacing d. Determine wavelength from lambda equals d sine theta over n. Repeat for several orders or both sides to check and average results. The structure and use of a spectrometer are not required.

Increasing frequency decreases wavelength, so more integer orders may satisfy n lambda is less than or equal to d. D makes d smaller and tends to reduce the available orders.

In one breath.
A diffraction grating produces sharp maxima at angles fixed by its line spacing and the light's wavelength. Measure an angle for a known diffraction order to determine the wavelength.
Key ideas.

A diffraction grating has many equally spaced lines or slits. The distance d between adjacent lines is the grating spacing. When light is incident normally, the central bright spot is the zero order maximum, n equals zero. First order maxima appear symmetrically on either side, followed by higher integer orders if geometry allows. The diffraction angle theta is measured from the central, straight through direction to one maximum, never from one side of the pattern to the other.
Constructive interference from adjacent slits requires a path difference of n lambda. That path difference is d sine theta, giving the diffraction grating equation.
d sine theta equals n lambda.

Here lambda is wavelength and n is a whole number diffraction order. If a grating has N lines per metre, d equals one over N metres. For a label in lines per millimetre, first multiply by one thousand to get lines per metre. For example, three hundred lines per millimetre means N equals three hundred thousand per metre and d equals three point three three times ten to the minus six metres.

Because sine theta is less than or equal to one, a maximum is possible only if n lambda is less than or equal to d. The largest possible integer order is the whole number part of d over lambda. If the pattern is visible on both sides, the number of maxima is two n sub the maximum of, plus one, including the central maximum. Whether a flat screen actually catches every possible order depends on its size.

The wave shows the electric field of monochromatic light at one instant. The labelled crest to crest distance lambda is one wavelength, this is the quantity determined using d sine theta equals n lambda. The sketch is schematic, with no numerical scale.
Method.

Direct a narrow monochromatic beam normally onto a grating of known line density. Place a screen beyond it, or observe the angular positions directly. Identify the central maximum and a matching pair of order n maxima. The structure and use of a spectrometer are not needed.

Measure the angle from the central direction to one maximum. If you measure the angle between the matching pair, halve it. With a flat screen, measure its distance L from the grating and the transverse distance y from centre to one maximum, then theta equals inverse tangent of open bracket y over L close bracket.

Convert line density into spacing d in metres. Calculate lambda equals d sine theta over n. Repeat using both sides and available orders, then average consistent values. State the wavelength in metres or nanometres with sensible significant figures.
Optional graph method.

For the same monochromatic light and grating, measure theta for several orders. Plot order n on the vertical axis against sine theta on the horizontal axis. Rearranging the grating equation gives n equals open bracket d over lambda close bracket sine theta, so the expected relationship is a straight line through the origin. Draw a line of best fit and determine its gradient G equals delta n over delta open bracket sine theta close bracket using widely separated points on the line. Hence G equals d over lambda and lambda equals d over G. Obtain d equals one over N from the line density N in lines per metre, convert lines per millimetre first.
Graph guidance, Cambridge Physics syllabus two thousand and twenty five to two thousand and twenty seven, pp.46 and fifty four, best fit lines and gradients.

This is six hundred and forty three nanometres.
Traps.
Trap, Use the angle between symmetric maxima as theta. Why it's wrong, The equation uses the angle from the centre to one maximum. Instead, Halve the full angle first.
Trap, Use y over L as sine theta. Why it's wrong, Screen geometry gives y over L equals tangent theta. Instead, Find theta with inverse tangent, then take its sine.
Trap, Treat three hundred lines per millimetre as d equals three hundred millimetres. Why it's wrong, Line density and spacing are reciprocals. Instead, Convert to lines per metre and invert.
Trap, Count only the positive orders. Why it's wrong, The pattern also has negative orders and zero order. Instead, Count both sides and the centre.
